quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “exactly” is typical in “That’s exactly what I meant”?
options: “exac-tly”: the /k/, /t/ and /l/ are all fully released in sequence
“exa-ktly”: the /k/ moves onto the next syllable and the /t/ is kept
“exac’ly”: the /t/ is left out between the /k/ and the /l/
“ex-ly”: both the /k/ and the /t/ are dropped
quests.correctAnswer: “exac’ly”: the /t/ is left out between the /k/ and the /l/
quests.hint: Say “exactly” slowly, then as you would in conversation. Count how many consonants you produce in a row after the vowel.
quests.explanation: “Exactly” contains the cluster /ktl/, which is hard to say quickly. The middle /t/ is the easiest sound to lose, so you often hear “exac’ly”. The /k/ and the /l/ stay, so the word is still recognisable. Three-consonant clusters are a classic place for elision.
quests.phoneticRule: In a sequence of three consonants, the middle stop is the usual casualty: /t/ is often omitted between /k/ and /l/ in words such as “exactly”.

quests.instruction: Which description fits “friendly” in “They’re very friendly people” when said quickly?
options: “frien’ly”: the /d/ is left out in the middle of the /ndl/ cluster
“fren-dly”: the /n/, /d/ and /l/ are all fully pronounced in a row
“fre-dly”: the /n/ is left out and the /d/ is kept
“frend-ly”: the /d/ moves onto the “ly” syllable
quests.correctAnswer: “frien’ly”: the /d/ is left out in the middle of the /ndl/ cluster
quests.hint: Listen to the middle of “friendly”: after the /n/, does a separate /d/ burst appear before the /l/?
quests.explanation: In /ndl/ the /d/ sits between a nasal and a /l/, made at almost the same place. That makes it very easy to skip, so “friendly” is often heard as “frien’ly”. The word is still clear because the /n/ and the /l/ remain.
quests.phoneticRule: The stop in a nasal + stop + /l/ cluster (as in /ndl/) is commonly omitted in casual speech, simplifying the cluster.

quests.instruction: Which sound is most likely to be missing in “next door” in “They live next door”?
options: The /k/ before the /s/
The /s/ in the middle of the cluster
The /d/ at the start of “door”
The /t/ between the /s/ and the /d/ of “door”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ between the /s/ and the /d/ of “door”
quests.hint: Write the consonants at the boundary: /k/, /s/, /t/, then /d/, and decide which of them is the weakest link.
quests.explanation: Four consonants meet at “next door”. The /t/ is the stop wedged in the middle, and it is also made at the same place as the following /d/, so it is easily lost: “nex’ door”. The other consonants help to keep the two words distinct.
quests.phoneticRule: In a long cluster across a word boundary, an alveolar stop between a fricative and another alveolar is the sound most often omitted.

quests.instruction: In “Sam missed lunch again”, which spoken form shows elision of the past-tense ending?
options: “mist lunch”: the /t/ is released clearly into the /l/, so “missed” sounds like “mist”
“miss lunch”: the /t/ is often left out, so “missed” can sound like “miss”
“miss-t lunch”: the /t/ moves onto the start of “lunch”
“miss-id lunch”: the ending becomes a full syllable with a vowel
quests.correctAnswer: “miss lunch”: the /t/ is often left out, so “missed” can sound like “miss”
quests.hint: Say “missed lunch” and “miss lunch” one after the other, and notice how different they sound at conversation speed.
quests.explanation: The past-tense ending of “missed” is a /t/ after /s/. Before “lunch” it sits in a crowded cluster, so it is often omitted: “miss’ lunch”. The listener then relies on context, such as “yesterday” or “again”, to know the verb is past.
quests.phoneticRule: The regular past-tense ending /t/ after a voiceless consonant is vulnerable to omission before a following consonant, so tense may be signalled by context rather than by the ending.

quests.instruction: Why can “worked hard” sound like “work hard” in fast speech?
options: Past-tense endings are silent in casual speech, so there is no difference at all between the two
The past-tense /t/ is easily lost between /k/ and /h/, so the forms can sound alike
The /k/ is dropped instead of the /t/, leaving something like “wor’ed”
The /h/ of “hard” moves back and replaces the /t/ of “worked”
quests.correctAnswer: The past-tense /t/ is easily lost between /k/ and /h/, so the forms can sound alike
quests.hint: Compare “work hard” and “worked hard”. What small sound is the only difference?
quests.explanation: The only difference between the two forms is a /t/, and that /t/ is squeezed between /k/ and /h/. It is easily lost, so listeners often rely on time words and context (“today”, “yesterday”) rather than on the ending itself. Knowing this prevents confusion between present and past in fast speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Regular past-tense endings /t/ and /d/ are frequently omitted after consonants before a following consonant, so tense is often signalled by context.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “stopped for” shows the same elision in “Dad stopped for petrol”?
options: “stopped for”, with a clear /t/ released into the /f/ of “for”
“stoppid for”: the ending becomes a full vowel and a /d/
“stob for”: the /t/ becomes a /b/ made at the lips
“stop’ for”: the past-tense /t/ is left out after the /p/ before “for”
quests.correctAnswer: “stop’ for”: the past-tense /t/ is left out after the /p/ before “for”
quests.hint: Look at what ends “stopped”: a /p/ followed by a /t/. Then notice that “for” begins with an /f/.
quests.explanation: “Stopped” ends in /pt/, and “for” begins with a consonant. The /t/ ending is therefore likely to be omitted, giving “stop’ for”. The same pattern applies to regular verbs whose stems end in a voiceless consonant, so it is a pattern worth learning, not a single case.
quests.phoneticRule: The pattern generalises to regular verbs with voiceless stems: the final /t/ of the past-tense ending is the part most likely to be omitted before a consonant.

quests.instruction: You leave a message: “Tell him I’ll call back.” Which spoken form of “tell him” is typical in fluent speech?
options: “te-lim”: the /h/ of “him” is left out, and the /l/ links to the vowel
“tell … him”: a clear /h/ is pronounced after a short pause between the words
“tell-chim”: the /h/ turns into a “ch” sound when the words are joined
“te-im”: the /l/ is dropped instead of the /h/
quests.correctAnswer: “te-lim”: the /h/ of “him” is left out, and the /l/ links to the vowel
quests.hint: Say “tell him” quickly and notice what the last sound of “tell” seems to start.
quests.explanation: In casual speech the /h/ of weak pronouns such as “him” is often left out when the word follows another word. “Him” then begins with a vowel, so the /l/ of “tell” links to it: “te-lim”. This is how elision opens the door for the linking you studied earlier.
quests.phoneticRule: The /h/ of an unstressed pronoun is commonly omitted mid-sentence, which creates a vowel-initial word that the previous consonant can link to.

quests.instruction: Why does “her” in “Give her a ring” sound as if it has no /h/?
options: The word “her” is replaced by the word “a” in casual speech, so no /h/ is expected
The /v/ of “give” is dropped and the /h/ of “her” is kept in its place
“Her” is unstressed, so its /h/ is easily lost and it links to the word before
“Her” is stressed in this phrase, which makes its first sound disappear
quests.correctAnswer: “Her” is unstressed, so its /h/ is easily lost and it links to the word before
quests.hint: Say “give her a ring” as one smooth chunk and notice where the /v/ ends up.
quests.explanation: Pronouns are normally unstressed, and an unstressed /h/ is often lost: “give-er”. The /v/ of “give” then links onto the vowel of “her”: “gi-ver”. A stressed “HER”, as in “give HER a ring, not him”, keeps its /h/.
quests.phoneticRule: Unstressed forms of pronouns lose /h/ readily, whereas stressed forms keep it; the stress pattern decides which form occurs.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “see his” in “Did you see his email?” shows the /h/ dropping and a link?
options: “see … his email”: the /h/ is kept clearly after a short pause between the words
“see-yiz email”: the /h/ of “his” is left out and a /j/ glide links the vowels together
“see-sis email”: the /h/ turns into an /s/
“sees email”: the /h/ and the vowel are both dropped, leaving only a /z/
quests.correctAnswer: “see-yiz email”: the /h/ of “his” is left out and a /j/ glide links the vowels together
quests.hint: Remember the glide you learned for vowels like the one in “see”. What would join it to “his” once the /h/ is gone?
quests.explanation: When the /h/ of “his” is omitted, “see” ends in a vowel and “his” begins with one, so the glide /j/ links them: “see-yiz”. Two earlier ideas, elision and glide linking, are working together here.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision of /h/ in weak forms creates new vowel + vowel boundaries, which are then linked by glides as in other connected speech.

quests.instruction: Predict how “and” is usually said in “fish and chips” at normal speed.
options: A weak “and” with the /d/ clearly released before the /tʃ/ of “chips”
“And” with a long stressed vowel, to mark the items in the list
Just the /d/, with the /n/ and the vowel dropped
A weak /n/, with the vowel and the /d/ both gone: “fish ’n’ chips”
quests.correctAnswer: A weak /n/, with the vowel and the /d/ both gone: “fish ’n’ chips”
quests.hint: Listen for the small word between “fish” and “chips”, and count how many of its three sounds you actually hear.
quests.explanation: “And” is a weak, unstressed word. In fast speech its vowel and its /d/ are often lost, leaving only a short /n/ that joins the word before: “fish ’n’ chips”. Because only the /n/ remains, learners who listen for the full word “and” sometimes miss it entirely.
quests.phoneticRule: The function word “and” is typically reduced to a syllabic or very short /n/ between two content words, losing both its vowel and its final /d/.

quests.instruction: Why is “and” so often reduced to /n/ in “salt and pepper”?
options: “And” is weak and unstressed, so its vowel and /d/ are easily lost between stressed words
“And” is just an older spelling variant of the single-letter word “n”
The /d/ of “and” is replaced by the /p/ of “pepper” that follows it
Speakers dislike the sound /d/ before /p/, so they remove it whenever the next word begins with that sound
quests.correctAnswer: “And” is weak and unstressed, so its vowel and /d/ are easily lost between stressed words
quests.hint: Think about which words in “salt and pepper” carry the stress, and which one does not.
quests.explanation: In English, stress and weak forms work together: the words that carry the meaning (“salt” and “pepper”) are stressed, and the small word between them is reduced. That reduction can remove the vowel and the /d/ of “and”, leaving “salt ’n’ pepper”. The /p/ plays no part in it.
quests.phoneticRule: Reduction of function words follows stress: unstressed “and” between stressed content words loses its vowel and /d/ more readily than a stressed or phrase-final “and”.

quests.instruction: Apply the idea: which spoken form of “and” fits “rock and roll”?
options: “rock ’n’ roll”: “and” is reduced to a short /n/ between the two stressed words
“rock and roll”, with a full /æ/ in “and” and a clearly released /d/
“rock-kand roll”: the /k/ of “rock” moves onto a fully pronounced “and”
“rock roll”: the word “and” is deleted completely, with no trace left
quests.correctAnswer: “rock ’n’ roll”: “and” is reduced to a short /n/ between the two stressed words
quests.hint: The title is famous in its reduced form. Say it the way it appears on posters and in song names.
quests.explanation: “Rock ’n’ roll” is such a common phrase that its reduced form is even written with apostrophes. The vowel and the /d/ of “and” are gone, and a short /n/ links the two stressed words. Seeing the reduced spelling in names helps you recognise the pattern in everyday speech.
quests.phoneticRule: Frequent fixed phrases often have their reduced forms lexicalised, which makes the reduced pronunciation of “and” more regular than in free combinations.

quests.instruction: Say “family” in “My family lives nearby”. How many syllables do you often hear?
options: Three: every vowel is pronounced, even in casual speech
Four: speakers add an extra vowel before the /l/
Two: “fam’ly”, with the weak middle vowel left out
One: “fam”, with the rest of the word dropped
quests.correctAnswer: Two: “fam’ly”, with the weak middle vowel left out
quests.hint: Tap your finger once for each syllable you actually say when you speak at normal speed.
quests.explanation: “Family” has three written syllables, but the weak vowel between /m/ and /l/ is often omitted, so it sounds like “fam’ly”. The stressed first syllable and the last syllable stay clear. Hearing two syllables instead of three is normal and does not change the meaning.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak vowels between a nasal and /l/ in unstressed syllables are frequently omitted, shortening the word by one syllable.

quests.instruction: Which syllable is most likely to be missing in “chocolate” in “Dark chocolate is healthier”?
options: The first syllable “choc”, so it sounds like “late”
The last syllable “late”, so it sounds like “choc-o”
The stressed vowel in “choc”, so it sounds like “ch-colate”
The weak middle syllable, so it sounds like “chock-lit”
quests.correctAnswer: The weak middle syllable, so it sounds like “chock-lit”
quests.hint: Say the word at normal speed. Which syllable is the quietest and shortest?
quests.explanation: “Chocolate” is written with three syllables, but the second one is weak and is often lost: “chock-lit”. The stressed first syllable and the final syllable remain, which is why the word is still easy to recognise. Many food words show the same shortening.
quests.phoneticRule: A weak syllable between a stressed syllable and the final syllable is a typical site of syllable elision in common words.

quests.instruction: Apply the idea to “different” in “Try a different route.” Which spoken form is typical?
options: “dif-fer-ent”: three syllables, each of them fully pronounced in casual speech
“diff’rent”: two syllables, with the weak vowel after the /f/ left out
“dif-ent”: the /r/ is dropped and the vowel is kept
“di-ferent”: the first /f/ is dropped
quests.correctAnswer: “diff’rent”: two syllables, with the weak vowel after the /f/ left out
quests.hint: Compare how many syllables are written with how many you say when you ask for directions quickly.
quests.explanation: “Different” loses the weak vowel after /f/ in casual speech and is often said as “diff’rent”. The /r/ stays, which keeps the word recognisable. Reductions like this are ordinary and appear in everyday speech and broadcasts.
quests.phoneticRule: Weak vowels before /r/ in unstressed syllables are often omitted, so the written syllable count overstates the spoken one.

quests.instruction: At a café you ask for “a cup of tea”. Which spoken form of “of” is typical before “tea”?
options: “cup-a tea”: the /v/ is left out and “of” is reduced to a weak vowel
“cup-ov tea”: the /v/ is pronounced fully before the /t/ of “tea”, with no reduction
“cup-off tea”: the /v/ becomes an /f/
“cup tea”: the whole word “of” disappears
quests.correctAnswer: “cup-a tea”: the /v/ is left out and “of” is reduced to a weak vowel
quests.hint: Say “cup of tea” as quickly as you would at a counter. Listen for the last sound of “of”.
quests.explanation: “Of” is a weak word, and before a consonant its /v/ is often omitted, leaving only a weak vowel: “cup-a tea”. The sound is so short that it is easy to miss, but it is still there. Recognising it prevents you from thinking that the word “of” has gone altogether.
quests.phoneticRule: The /v/ of “of” is commonly omitted before a following consonant, leaving a weak vowel /ə/.

quests.instruction: Why is “could have” often written wrongly as “could of”?
options: Because “of” and “have” mean the same in English
Because the /v/ is pronounced twice in the phrase, which makes it look like the word “of” on the page
The reduced spoken form /kʊdə/ has lost its /v/, so it sounds like “could uh”
Because “have” is replaced by “of” in fast speech
quests.correctAnswer: The reduced spoken form /kʊdə/ has lost its /v/, so it sounds like “could uh”
quests.hint: Say “could have” in a fast, relaxed way and listen to the sound where “have” should be.
quests.explanation: In casual speech “could have” is reduced to /kʊdə/: the /h/ and the /v/ of “have” are both lost, and a weak vowel is left. That weak vowel sounds like the reduced form of “of”, so some writers wrongly spell “could of”. The grammar needs “have”, whatever the pronunciation.
quests.phoneticRule: Reduced “have” (/əv/ or /ə/) sounds the same as reduced “of”, which is the source of the common spelling error “could of”.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “most of the time” fits “It happens most of the time”?
quests.word: It happens most of the time
quests.textToSpeak: It happens most of the time
options: “mos’ of the time”: the /t/ is left out and the /v/ is kept
“mo-stov the time”: the /t/ links onto “of” and the /v/ is fully pronounced
“mo-sta the time”: the /t/ links onto “of”, and the /v/ is left out
“mo’ the time”: the /s/, the /t/ and “of” all disappear
quests.correctAnswer: “mo-sta the time”: the /t/ links onto “of”, and the /v/ is left out
quests.hint: Two different processes meet here: one sound links forward, and one sound is lost. Decide which is which.
quests.explanation: The /t/ of “most” is followed by the vowel of “of”, so it links onto it. The /v/ of “of” is followed by the consonant /ð/, so it is often lost. You therefore hear “mo-sta the time”, with a link and an omission in the same chunk.
quests.phoneticRule: In “of” + consonant sequences, the preceding consonant may link to the vowel of “of” while the /v/ itself is omitted.

quests.instruction: In a team chat you hear “Send the next batch tomorrow.” Which sound is likely missing in “next batch”?
options: The /k/ at the start of the cluster
The /t/ between the /s/ and the /b/
The /b/ at the start of “batch”
The /s/ before the /t/
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ between the /s/ and the /b/
quests.hint: At the boundary the consonants are /k/, /s/, /t/ and then /b/. Which is the stop wedged in the middle?
quests.explanation: Four consonants meet at “next batch”. The /t/ is the weak stop in the middle, so it is often omitted: “nex’ batch”. The /s/ and the /b/ remain, so the listener can still tell the words apart. Workplace messages are said quickly, so this reduced form is typical.
quests.phoneticRule: In /kst/ + consonant sequences the /t/ is most often omitted, while the fricative and the following consonant remain.

quests.instruction: Which two /t/ sounds are most likely to be omitted in “Kim tested the first plan last week”?
quests.word: Kim tested the first plan last week
quests.textToSpeak: Kim tested the first plan last week
options: The /t/ at the start of “tested” and the /t/ of “first”
The /t/ at the start of “tested” and the /t/ of “last”
The /t/ in the middle of “tested” and the /t/ of “first”
The /t/ of “first” and the /t/ of “last”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “first” and the /t/ of “last”
quests.hint: Only a /t/ that ends a word, sits after /s/ and is followed by a consonant is at risk. Find two of them.
quests.explanation: “First” ends in /st/ before the /p/ of “plan”, and “last” ends in /st/ before the /w/ of “week”. Both /t/ sounds sit in crowded clusters and are often omitted: “firs’ plan las’ week”. The /t/ at the start of “tested” and the one in its middle are in positions that need to be pronounced.
quests.phoneticRule: Word-final /t/ after /s/ before a consonant is the principal elision site; word-initial and pre-vocalic /t/ are normally kept.
quests.spokenForm: Kim tested the firs’ plan las’ week

quests.instruction: A client says “It’s our biggest risk now.” Which spoken form of “biggest risk” is typical?
options: “biggis’ risk”: the /t/ is omitted after the /s/ and before the /r/ of “risk”
“bigges-trisk”: the /t/ moves onto “risk” and the /s/ is kept apart
“biggest … risk”: the /t/ is released with a clear puff of air
“bigger risk”: the /s/ and /t/ are both replaced by an /r/
quests.correctAnswer: “biggis’ risk”: the /t/ is omitted after the /s/ and before the /r/ of “risk”
quests.hint: Write the consonants at the boundary: /s/, /t/, then /r/. Decide which sound is most likely to be missing.
quests.explanation: “Biggest” ends in /st/, and “risk” begins with /r/. The /t/ is wedged between /s/ and /r/, so it is often left out: “biggis’ risk”. Business talk uses many superlatives such as “biggest”, “best” and “highest”, so the pattern is worth recognising.
quests.phoneticRule: Superlative endings in /st/ commonly lose the /t/ before a consonant, as in “biggest risk” and similar phrases.

quests.instruction: A learner says every sound in “Please spell your last name” clearly in an interview. Is that a problem?
options: Yes: the /t/ must be dropped in fast speech, or the speech will sound foreign to the interviewer
Yes: a fully pronounced /t/ makes the sentence ungrammatical and unnatural
No, but only if the learner also writes the sentence down with the /t/ omitted
No: a clearly pronounced /t/ is acceptable; omission is an option, not a requirement
quests.correctAnswer: No: a clearly pronounced /t/ is acceptable; omission is an option, not a requirement
quests.hint: Ask whether elision is a rule that every speaker must follow, or a tendency that depends on speed and style.
quests.explanation: Elision is a tendency of fast, relaxed speech. Pronouncing the /t/ clearly in “last name” is natural, especially in an interview, and listeners understand it easily. What the learner needs is to recognise the omitted version when others say it, not to copy it all the time.
quests.phoneticRule: Elision is optional and style-dependent; full forms remain acceptable in careful and formal speech, so recognition matters more than production.

quests.instruction: A student writes “Mum miss the las bus” because that is how it sounds. What is the best advice?
options: Write exactly what you hear, because English spelling is supposed to follow pronunciation letter by letter
Spelling follows the full written forms, so keep “missed” and “last” even if speech omits the /t/
Use the reduced forms in formal reports, because they are more natural and match speech
Remove every /t/ in writing, since speech has already lost them in this phrase
quests.correctAnswer: Spelling follows the full written forms, so keep “missed” and “last” even if speech omits the /t/
quests.hint: Think about what a reader needs, compared with what a listener needs.
quests.explanation: Speech and spelling work on different systems. A listener hears “miss’” and “las’” and uses context to understand; a reader needs the full forms to see tense and word identity. So write “missed” and “last”, and keep the reductions for pronunciation.
quests.phoneticRule: Spelling represents word identity and grammar, not the connected-speech realisation, so elision does not change how words are written.

quests.instruction: At a formal presentation you say “Our first question is price.” Which delivery of “first question” is the safest choice?
options: Omit the /t/ as often as possible, because omission sounds more fluent and professional to every listener
Pronounce every word with long pauses between them so that nothing is reduced
Either form is acceptable, but a clear /t/ at a natural pace is the safest in formal speech
Replace the /t/ with a throat stop to sound casual and relaxed in front of the audience
quests.correctAnswer: Either form is acceptable, but a clear /t/ at a natural pace is the safest in formal speech
quests.hint: Think about audience and context: a formal talk, listeners who need to follow every point.
quests.explanation: In formal speech both the reduced and the full forms are possible, but a clear /t/ at a natural pace does not risk confusion. Over-slow delivery with long pauses sounds stiff, and deliberate casual reductions can sound out of place. So choose clarity first, and let natural linking happen on its own.
quests.phoneticRule: Register affects the degree of reduction: formal speech tends to retain more segments, but it still uses linking and natural rhythm.

quests.instruction: Predict which sound may go missing in “hand luggage” at an airport check-in.
options: The /d/ at the end of “hand”
The /n/ in the middle of “hand”
The /l/ at the start of “luggage”
The /g/ in the middle of “luggage”
quests.correctAnswer: The /d/ at the end of “hand”
quests.hint: Look at the cluster that ends “hand”: decide which of its two sounds is the stop, and what comes next.
quests.explanation: “Hand” ends in /nd/ and “luggage” begins with /l/, so the /d/ is wedged between a nasal and another consonant. It is the sound most likely to be omitted: “han’ luggage”. Airport staff say this phrase quickly many times a day, so the reduced form is very common.
quests.phoneticRule: Word-final /nd/ before a consonant tends to lose the /d/, keeping the nasal that signals the word.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form of “direct” fits “Book a direct flight tonight”?
options: “direct flight”: the /t/ is released with a puff of air before the /f/
“direc’ flight”: the /t/ is omitted between the /k/ and the /f/
“direc-tflight”: the /t/ moves onto “flight”
“dire flight”: the /k/ and /t/ are both omitted
quests.correctAnswer: “direc’ flight”: the /t/ is omitted between the /k/ and the /f/
quests.hint: Say “direct flight” at the pace of a booking call. Notice whether you stop the air for a /t/ before the /f/ begins.
quests.explanation: “Direct” ends in /kt/ and “flight” begins with /f/, so the /t/ is again between other consonants. It is often omitted: “direc’ flight”. The /k/ remains, which keeps “direct” distinct from “dire”. Travel bookings contain many phrases like this.
quests.phoneticRule: The /kt/ cluster loses its /t/ before a consonant in travel and business vocabulary just as readily as in everyday words.

quests.instruction: Which statement explains the missing sound in “Read the most recent message”?
options: The /m/ of “most” is dropped because the word “recent” follows it
The /s/ is dropped and the /t/ is kept, so it sounds like “mot recent”
The /r/ of “recent” moves back onto “most”
The /t/ sits between /s/ and /r/ and is often omitted, giving “mos’ recent”
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ sits between /s/ and /r/ and is often omitted, giving “mos’ recent”
quests.hint: Write the consonants where the two words meet: /s/, /t/ and /r/. Which is the weakest of the three?
quests.explanation: “Most” ends in /st/, and “recent” begins with /r/. The /t/ is the stop wedged in the middle, so it is often omitted: “mos’ recent”. The prediction rule you have practised, looking for /t/ or /d/ between two other consonants, works for a new phrase just as well.
quests.phoneticRule: Prediction rule: scan for a word-final /t/ or /d/ that follows another consonant and precedes a consonant; that sound is the likely omission.

quests.instruction: Which statement is accurate for the /t/ sounds in “Mum asked about the next bus”?
quests.word: Mum asked about the next bus
quests.textToSpeak: Mum asked about the next bus
options: The /t/ of “asked” is omitted before “about”, and the /t/ of “next” links onto “bus”
Both /t/ sounds are omitted
The /t/ of “next” is omitted before “bus”, while the /t/ of “asked” links onto the vowel of “about”
Neither /t/ is affected, because each one is followed by a clear boundary between words
quests.correctAnswer: The /t/ of “next” is omitted before “bus”, while the /t/ of “asked” links onto the vowel of “about”
quests.hint: For each /t/, check what sound follows it: a vowel or a consonant.
quests.explanation: The /t/ of “asked” is followed by the vowel of “about”, so it links: “ask-ta-bout”. The /t/ of “next” is followed by the consonant /b/, so it is often omitted: “nex’ bus”. One sentence shows both outcomes, chosen by the following sound.
quests.phoneticRule: The next sound selects the outcome for a word-final /t/: a vowel gives linking, a consonant makes elision possible.

quests.instruction: Which pair of reductions is heard in “Cheese and crackers, mostly”?
options: “And” is reduced to /n/, and the /t/ of “mostly” is omitted
“And” is deleted entirely, and the /t/ of “mostly” moves onto “ly”
The /s/ of “cheese” is omitted, and “crackers” loses its first syllable
Only “and” is reduced; “mostly” keeps all its sounds
quests.correctAnswer: “And” is reduced to /n/, and the /t/ of “mostly” is omitted
quests.hint: Check each reduction in turn: one affects a small word, the other a cluster inside a word.
quests.explanation: “And” between two content words is reduced to a short /n/. In “mostly”, the /t/ is wedged between /s/ and /l/ and is often omitted: “mos’ly”. So the same phrase shows a weak-word reduction and a cluster simplification.
quests.phoneticRule: Function-word reduction and consonant-cluster simplification are separate processes, and both can occur within a single short phrase.

quests.instruction: Which spoken form fits “The last train might have gone” in fast speech?
quests.word: The last train might have gone
quests.textToSpeak: The last train might have gone
options: “The last train might have gone”, with every sound clearly released, as in slow and careful speech
“The las’ train might-a gone”: the /t/ of “last” is omitted and the /v/ of “have” is lost
“The las-ttrain might have gone”: the /t/ moves onto “train”
“The last train migh’ have gone”: the /t/ of “might” is omitted and the rest is clear
quests.correctAnswer: “The las’ train might-a gone”: the /t/ of “last” is omitted and the /v/ of “have” is lost
quests.hint: Look for one /t/ before a consonant and one small word whose /v/ may disappear.
quests.explanation: “Last” ends in /st/ before the /t/ of “train”, so its /t/ is often omitted, and “have” is reduced to a weak vowel after “might”: “The las’ train might-a gone”. Combining both gives the typical fast form. Note that the written form is still “might have”.
quests.phoneticRule: Several reductions can occur in one sentence; each is driven by its own context: cluster simplification for /t/ and weak-form reduction for “have”.
